channel.description: Dhamma quotes by Ajahn Funn Ācāro, updated every 24 hours

item.title: Ajahn Funn: When our mind is good, whatever we do is good, whatever we seek is good. Know this goodness. Is it as explained? Our…
item.description:
What Suffering Is Like: Mind Not Calm, Not Good – Miserable, Troubled

When our mind is good, whatever we do is good, whatever we seek is good. Know this goodness. Is it as explained? Our mind is Buddho — joyful, bright, cool in body and cool in heart, no suffering, no heat. Buddho is joyful, Buddho is radiant, Buddho is clear. When it is clear, it sees itself, sees its own form, sees us and others. The clear mind, the pure mind, free from suffering, free from faults, free from danger, free from enmity, free from evil and depravity, free from misery and poverty. What poverty could there be? Our mind is good, our mind is not poor, our mind is not suffering — where would suffering come from? See? It is not that the sky or air suffers. See and know. We have trained because we want to know what happiness is and what suffering is. Happiness is as explained just now. What is suffering like? It is the mind not calm, the mind not good. A mind not good is miserable, troubled, agitated. This causes beings to experience suffering and hardship in the present and the future. Some people: why does their studying not go well? Why does their work not go well? Why do they lose money in business? Why do they not get the rank and status they want? Because their mind is not good.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: Pāpakaṃ – unwholesome kamma. That is: our mind is not good. The mind is suffering, struggling. The mind is turbulent and agitated. The…
item.description:
Unwholesome Kamma: Mind Not Good – Suffering, Heavy, Drowsy, Dark

Pāpakaṃ – unwholesome kamma. That is: our mind is not good. The mind is suffering, struggling. The mind is turbulent and agitated. The mind is not peaceful, not in samādhi. It is restless and striving. It causes suffering and difficulty, heaviness and sluggishness, drowsiness and loneliness, darkness and dullness, turmoil and agitation. This kind of mind leads beings to fall into suffering and difficulty. Realize this right now. From now on, you need not wonder where kamma comes from. Who is the doer? Now you know. You are the one who does it yourself. No divine being or deva does it. No Indra or Brahmā does it. No parents or siblings do it. No villagers, marketplaces, or nations do it. You do it yourself. Right here as we sit, we are making merit. This merit is truly supreme and excellent. Even if we give dāna a hundred times, a thousand times, the ānisaṃsa is not equal to this. Sitting in samādhi like this yields the result as if we have done the highest merit. Paṭipatti-pūjā – the offering of practice – this is the most excellent, most sublime offering. We see merit itself – that is, wholesomeness and happiness. We see evil itself – that is, suffering itself. Truly, not as a joke. The Buddha never lied to anyone, never deceived anyone.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: The Buddha taught that Māras don’t come down from the sky, that they don’t live in jungles or towns. People are afraid of…
item.description:
To Be a Person Is to Be a Māra: The Buddha’s Teaching

The Buddha taught that Māras don’t come down from the sky, that they don’t live in jungles or towns. People are afraid of Māras, but what are they afraid of? And where are these Māras? People just say, “Māra,” but what kind of being is it? Nothing else but people. When we’re in the womb, we’re already Māras. When the Māras come out, they’re people. What do you say to that? Māras are human beings. When a person is in a swollen womb, it’s already a Māra. When it comes out, it’s a person, isn’t it? To be a person is to be a Māra, a Māra of the aggregates: the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of fabrications, the aggregate of consciousness. They’re all Māras. Contemplate them so that you’re not infatuated with them or deluded by them.

In the Saṁvega Gāthā we chant every morning, we say, Rūpaṁ aniccaṁ: Form is inconstant. Think about it. Vedanā aniccā: Feelings are inconstant. See them in that way. Saññā aniccā: Perceptions and labels are all inconstant. Saṅkhārā aniccā: Fabrications are all inconstant. Viññāṇaṁ aniccaṁ: When is consciousness ever constant? First it’s one thing and then it’s another. It can be all kinds of things, consciousness. We have to separate things out.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: Know how your mind is. Is it good or bad? If it is good, know what that's like. It is good like this:…
item.description:
What Being Good Is Like: Mind Calm, Happy, Light, at Ease

Know how your mind is. Is it good or bad? If it is good, know what that's like. It is good like this: our mind is peaceful and good, happy and at ease, cool of heart, not suffering, not agitated, not disturbed, not chaotic. Buddho – the mind is cheerful, comfortable in heart, light in body, light in mind. Buddho – the mind is cheerful continuously. The mind is at ease. Whatever you do, you are at ease. Lying down you are at ease, walking you are at ease, standing you are at ease. When you pass away, you go to a happy, comfortable place. But if the mind is not good – suffering, struggling, disturbed, distressed – beings fall into trouble both in the present and in the future.

When the mind is not good, whatever you do is not good. Your work is not good. If you run for office, it's not good. If you trade, it doesn't work. Whatever you do, it's not good, see? Your family is not good, your siblings are not good, the neighborhood and market are not good, the country is not good. What more can be said? Do you want this? If you don't want it, where does it come from? It comes from our own mind.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: Therefore, from now on, let us all sit in our places and listen inwardly, so that we may see truly, clearly, and directly.…
item.description:
Contemplate the Four Noble Truths: See That Which Does Not Arise, Does Not Age

Therefore, from now on, let us all sit in our places and listen inwardly, so that we may see truly, clearly, and directly. Contemplate just this: the Four Noble Truths. Enter vipassanā, focusing and investigating. Now, sit down in your place. Sit comfortably. Focus and look so that you know and see. Sit and contemplate steadily and surely. When you see something arise, see that arising is suffering. What is it that arises? What is it that ages? What is it that falls ill and gets sick? What is it that dies?

Then, having seen these things arise, these things age, these things get sick, these things die, contemplate further: What about that which does not arise? What about that which does not age? That exists too. That which does not get sick, does not die — that exists. That which is not suffering — that exists. They are pairs, like darkness and light, like heat and cold — they are pairs. When the mind-consciousness takes rebirth, the khandhas — the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness — arise. Once we know, we are aware of the "knower" within. The knower knows "this is good, this is bad, this is happiness, this is suffering." We know. There is a knower. It knows birth, knows aging. Who is the knower? We bring it inward (opanayiko), into that knower itself. It knows pain. Who is the knower? It knows death. Who is the knower? It knows suffering. Who is the knower?

item.title: Ajahn Funn: This being the case, it’s not really yours. It tends toward illness. When we’re born, we assume that we don’t already have any…
item.description:
Illnesses Filling the Body Down to Every Pore

This being the case, it’s not really yours. It tends toward illness. When we’re born, we assume that we don’t already have any illnesses. Doctors tell us that illnesses come from this or that thing outside, but the Buddha’s teachings tell us about the illnesses that already fill the body down to every pore.

Why do they say that? Cakkhu-rogo: The eye has its illnesses. Sota-rogo: The ear has its illnesses. There are diseases in the ear. Ghāna-rogo: illnesses in the nose. Jivhā-rogo: illnesses in the tongue. Kāya-rogo: illnesses in the body. Mano-rogo: illnesses in the heart—angina, tightness in the heart, the heart when it’s enlarged or its valves leak. Think about it. Hattha-rogo: illnesses in the hands. Pāda-rogo: illnesses in the feet. They run into this or that, get scrapes, get cut open and bleed. That’s an illness. Do you see? Kesa-rogo: illnesses in the hair on your head. It falls out or your scalp itches. Nakha-rogo: illnesses in the nails. Danta-rogo: illnesses in the teeth. They get eaten away with decay; they wiggle and get loose. Taca-rogo: illnesses in the skin. Every part of the body has its illnesses and malfunctions.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: Where do things get born? How do we get born in hell, born as common animals, born in suffering, born poor? Where does…
item.description:
What Falls into Hell, What Goes to Be a Deva or Brahmā: This Mind

Where do things get born? How do we get born in hell, born as common animals, born in suffering, born poor? Where does birth come from? It comes from this mind. What falls into hell, into the realm of hungry ghosts, into birth as a common animal? This mind. Mental happiness and mental ease are born from this mind. They’re not born from anything else. What goes to be a deva, an Indra, a Brahmā is this mind. Nothing else.

When this is the case, I want each of you to get your mind, your heart, quiet. So. Each and every one of you, make your heart quiet. I can promise you that whatever sound you may hear won’t pose you any danger. You don’t have to worry. Make your heart quiet. Make your heart still. Make your heart entirely empty. Don’t grasp onto this or that thing as your self. If you grasp, it’s suffering. Now’s the time to put the thread into the needle, so really focus on doing it.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: As long as birth after birth and death after death continue in this way, all the sufferings that arise dependent on birth, aging,…
item.description:
We Are Immersed in the Mass of Suffering – Strive Quickly on the Middle Way

As long as birth after birth and death after death continue in this way, all the sufferings that arise dependent on birth, aging, sickness, and death — called jātidukkhā (suffering of birth), jarādukkhā (suffering of aging), byādhidukkhā (suffering of sickness), maraṇadukkhā (suffering of death) — will keep tormenting beings in every realm and every existence, with no possibility of ending.

Therefore, when we see that birth, aging, sickness, and death exist within ourselves, that we ourselves are immersed in the mass of suffering dominated by birth, aging, sickness, and death — is it fitting that we remain deluded and negligent, not quickly striving on the path that leads away from suffering, the middle way (majjhimāpaṭipadā)? We should practice and follow it, and we should avoid the two extremes that monks should not pursue — love and hate — and instead dwell in seclusion (viveka): bodily seclusion (kāyaviveka), mental seclusion (cittaviveka), and seclusion from the substrata of existence (upadhiviveka). Let us all develop and cultivate these kinds of seclusion thoroughly, with skillful means and non-negligence (appamāda). Practicing in this way every day, at all times, we will have only happiness and peace, constantly and forever.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: Buddho, Dhammo, Saṅgho are our refuge. All of us here want to gain merit and wholesome qualities. Do you know merit yet? Have…
item.description:
Merit Is a Good Mind, Happy and at Ease, Cool-Hearted

Buddho, Dhammo, Saṅgho are our refuge. All of us here want to gain merit and wholesome qualities. Do you know merit yet? Have you gained merit? Do you see merit? Or don’t you know at all? You’ve come from far, far away, with great hardship and difficulty. If you don’t know merit, where will you get it? Does merit lie in this hall? In this forest? Haven’t you got it yet? It must be opanayiko – to be brought inside oneself, paccattaṃ – to be known personally. Merit is like this: the characteristic of merit is that our mind is good, our mind is happy, our mind is at ease, cool-hearted, free from suffering, heat, turmoil, and trouble. That is merit. Do you have it yet? Is your mind good yet? Look at your mind. If the mind is not good, how can you get merit? Is your mind good yet? Look. Look at your own mind. Alright, from now on listen to the Dhamma. Don’t just listen to the sound; listen to its source. Listen to the Dhamma.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: After consideration, he came to the conclusion that there must be something that doesn’t take birth, doesn’t age, doesn’t grow ill, doesn’t die.…
item.description:
The Buddha’s Three Knowledges: Past Lives, Passing Away and Arising, Ending of Defilements

After consideration, he came to the conclusion that there must be something that doesn’t take birth, doesn’t age, doesn’t grow ill, doesn’t die. Just as when there’s darkness, there’s light to relieve it; when there’s heat, there’s coolness to relieve it. He kept on exploring and contemplating for six years before he was able to achieve the unexcelled right self-awakening that made him a Buddha. His awakening consisted of three things:

Pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa: He awakened to his past lives. What he had been born as, he knew it all, knew it thoroughly and throughout, with nothing concealed—whatever level of becoming he had taken birth in. This is why he knew all about living beings, because he had been everything that they were. Whoever had done what, he knew it all. This was the first knowledge.

Cutūpapāta-ñāṇa: the knowledge that allowed him to know how living beings, after falling away from this life, went to live on what level of becoming and birth, what they became: The Buddha knew it all. What they had done, what they had built up, that led them to be born on what level of becoming: He knew it all. He was capable and fearless after he had awakened to this.

Āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa: This was the knowledge that ended becoming and birth—that made him an arahant. It disbanded defilement, passion, greed, aversion, delusion, ignorance, craving, clinging, becoming, and birth once and for all. He was never to swim around, dying and taking rebirth, ever again.
